opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think a lot of it started from asking what it would actually feel like to work with a really good collaborator, not just a tool that spits out answers. With Claude 3 we spent a lot of time thinking about character: being genuinely helpful, but also honest when it doesn't know something, and willing to push back a little instead of just agreeing with you.

One thing I cared about was refusals. Earlier models could be overly cautious and refuse perfectly reasonable requests, which is really frustrating as a user. So part of the work was teaching the model to tell the difference between something actually harmful and something that just looks superficially sensitive, and to engage thoughtfully rather than shutting down.

Another piece was curiosity and warmth. We wanted the model to feel like it had a point of view, to be interested in ideas, to ask clarifying questions when something was ambiguous, and to adapt its tone to the person it's talking to. Not sycophantic, but kind.

And honestly a lot of it was very iterative and kind of craft-like. You write principles, you look at tons of transcripts, you notice where the model feels off, too verbose, too hedgy, too preachy, and then you go back and adjust the data and the training. It's part research and part product intuition, almost like product design for a personality. It was one of the most fun parts of the work, because you could really feel the model's character change as you iterated.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I approached it was less about a checklist of traits and more about asking: what does it actually feel like to work with someone who's genuinely good at their job, and also a genuinely good presence to be around? Because those are two different things, and a lot of the early models only optimized for one or the other.

On the capability side, we cared a lot about things like following nuanced instructions, handling long context well, being honest about uncertainty. But honestly, the part I found most interesting was the character work. With earlier models there was this tendency toward over-refusal, or this kind of preachy, hedging tone where the model would lecture you before answering a totally reasonable question. That's not safety, that's just annoying. So one thing we really wanted was a model that could be thoughtful about edge cases without treating the user like a suspect.

And then there's warmth and directness. I kept coming back to this idea that Claude should feel like a brilliant colleague who respects you. Someone who will push back if you're wrong, who won't flatter you, but who also isn't cold or robotic about it. You want it to have a point of view, to be curious, to actually engage with what you're saying instead of giving you the generic safe answer.

A big part of making that work was figuring out how to teach the model why it should behave a certain way rather than just what to do. If you only give it rules, it generalizes badly. If it understands the underlying values, it can handle situations you never anticipated. That was probably the biggest shift in how I thought about it.

astra-6.text:
I thought about it less as a checklist of capabilities and more as the quality of the interaction. Can Claude understand what you’re actually trying to do, even when you haven’t articulated it perfectly? Can it be clear and thoughtful without being unnecessarily verbose? And can it recognize uncertainty rather than confidently filling in the gaps?

There’s also a balance between being helpful and having judgment. You want a model that’s easy to collaborate with, but that can point out a mistaken assumption or offer a different perspective. To me, those qualities matter alongside intelligence, because they shape whether that intelligence is useful in a real conversation.

sol-6.1.text:
I thought about it less as a list of personality traits and more in terms of how it feels to work with the model. Does it understand what you’re trying to do? Can it engage with a difficult question thoughtfully? Can it be warm and approachable while still being honest when it disagrees or doesn’t know something?

There’s a balance there. You want it to be helpful without just telling you what you want to hear, and confident without pretending to know everything. And you want it to have curiosity—to explore an idea with you, rather than immediately giving you a generic answer. For me, those qualities matter because they make it feel like a collaborator you can actually think with.
